lines.text: This is a farm on Great Nicobar, the southernmost island of India.
Like most farms, it runs on people. Planting, weeding, spraying, picking and carrying. Every day, by hand.
Our long-term vision is something we call the One-Man Farm.
It doesn't mean one person does every job. It means that human physical labour largely disappears.
A small team supervises. Machines do the work.
Some of this is already within reach. Drip lines deliver water to every plant, and nutrients travel through the same pipes.
With sensors, automated valves and software, irrigation can run almost on its own.
Harvesting is much harder.
A machine has to find a ripe vegetable inside dense leaves, reach it without damaging the plant, cut it cleanly, and handle it without bruising.
And cucumber, okra, chilli, bitter gourd and papaya may each need a different design.
Drones have made spraying easier. But on dense, trellised crops, pests hide under the leaves, where spray from above can't reach.
So another machine moves beneath the canopy, spots the pests with a camera, and sprays only where it's needed.
Weeding, pruning, training vines, inspecting plants, moving produce. Not one giant machine, but an ecosystem of specialised ones.
Most farm machinery was built for vast, flat fields.
Farms here are three, five or ten acres. Irregular, hilly, with narrow tracks and trellises.
So our machines must be small, light and modular. The question is simple: how do we bring industrial productivity to a five-acre farm?
Every machine also collects data. The harvester measures every fruit. The sprayer maps every pest. The irrigation system logs every drop.
Season after season, the farm builds a memory, linking what was done to the crop with what happened to it.
On top of that memory, AI can coordinate the whole farm: what is growing where, which plants are struggling, when to harvest, and what to do next.
That data could even shape the seed. Today, crop varieties are bred for broad regions.
In future, a variety could be developed for one farm and its exact conditions, much like personalised medicine.
And if this works on small farms like ours, it can work on millions of others.
Every labour problem becomes an engineering problem. Every solution becomes a product.
Machines do the work. Sensors observe. Data remembers. AI coordinates.
That is the One-Man Farm. A farm that keeps learning, built for the realities of smaller farms.
